```{=html}
<header class="dg-head dg-head-section"><p class="dg-kicker">Chapter 3 <span class="dg-sep">•</span> <a href="index.html">Topological Manifolds</a></p><h1 class="dg-title"><span class="dg-secnum">3.3</span> Smooth Manifolds</h1></header>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>An atlas is <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple"><span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible</span>, denoted as <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\)</span>, if for any pair of charts <span class="math inline">\(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right), \left(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}\right) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\)</span>:</p>
<ol class="dg-enumerate dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Either <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \emptyset\)</span>, or</p></li>
<li><p><span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \neq \emptyset\)</span> and both chart transition maps, <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\)</span>, are <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span> functions in the “ordinary multivariable calculus sense”<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-4" id="fnref-4" aria-label="Footnote 4">4</a></sup>.</p></li>
</ol></li>
<li><p>A <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple"><span class="math inline">\(d\)</span>-dim. smooth manifold</span> (or <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-manifold)<sup class="dg-fnref"><a href="#fn-5" id="fnref-5" aria-label="Footnote 5">5</a></sup> is the triple <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, {\mathcal{A}}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul>
```

## `<span class="dg-secnum">3.3.1</span> Smooth Maps and Diffeomorphisms`{=html} {#subsection_Smooth_Maps_Diffeomorphisms}

```{=html}
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-1">
<li><p>Smoothness of maps is defined through charts, by reducing it to ordinary multivariable calculus. A function <span class="math inline">\(f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\)</span> on a smooth manifold <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\)</span> is <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple">smooth</span> if, for every chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\)</span>, its <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple">chart representative</span>  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}
        \end{align*}</span>  is <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span> in the ordinary multivariable calculus sense. This is where <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatibility becomes essential: if <span class="math inline">\(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\)</span> is smooth and <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\)</span> is another chart, then on <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V})\)</span>  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1}
            = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right)
            = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}},
        \end{align*}</span>  a composition of smooth maps, hence smooth. Smoothness checked in one chart around each point therefore holds in all charts: the notion is chart-independent. On a merely topological manifold, whose transition maps are only continuous, no such chart-independent notion of differentiability would exist.</p></li>
<li><p>More generally, given two smooth manifolds <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M} \right)_{d}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N} \right)_{e}\)</span>, a continuous map <span class="math inline">\(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\)</span> is <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple">smooth</span> if, for every pair of charts <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}\)</span>, its chart representative  <span class="math display">\begin{align*}
            \mathscr{Y} \circ \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} :
            \mathscr{X}\big( \mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V}) \big) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d
            \longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^e
        \end{align*}</span>  is <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>. Continuity of <span class="math inline">\(\phi\)</span> guarantees that <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V})\)</span> is open, so the representative is defined on an open subset of <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^d\)</span>, and the same composition argument as above shows that the notion is chart-independent. Two special cases will be used constantly:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p>smooth functions are the smooth maps into <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{N} = \mathbb{R}\)</span>, equipped with its standard smooth structure <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathbb{R}, \mathcal{O}_\mathbb{R}, \{ (\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}) \} \right)_1\)</span>;</p></li>
<li><p>smooth curves are the smooth maps <span class="math inline">\(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\)</span>, with <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}\)</span> carrying the same standard structure: <span class="math inline">\(\gamma\)</span> is smooth if and only if <span class="math inline">\(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\)</span> is <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span> on <span class="math inline">\(\mathrm{preim}_\gamma(\mathcal{U})\)</span> for every chart <span class="math inline">\((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\)</span>.</p></li>
</ul></li>
<li><p>A <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple">diffeomorphism</span> is a smooth bijection <span class="math inline">\(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\)</span> whose inverse <span class="math inline">\(\phi^{-1} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}\)</span> is also smooth. If one exists, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{M}\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{N}\)</span> are <span class="dg-term dg-term-purple">diffeomorphic</span>. Diffeomorphic manifolds are indistinguishable as smooth manifolds, just as homeomorphic spaces are indistinguishable as topological spaces, and isomorphic vector spaces as vector spaces. This is the notion of equivalence implicit in the footnote on exotic smooth structures above.</p></li>
</ul>
<div class="dg-footnotes"><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-4"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-4" aria-label="Back to the text">4</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>By “ordinary multivariable calculus sense” we mean that the transition maps, <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\)</span>, are smooth functions between open subsets of <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^d\)</span> in the usual calculus sense, i.e., they admit continuous partial derivatives of all orders.</p>
<p>Useful remarks:</p>
<ul class="dg-itemize dg-depth-2">
<li><p>Here we refer specifically to <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatibility, but the notion of compatibility extends naturally to any desired degree of differentiability (<span class="math inline">\(C^k\)</span>, <span class="math inline">\(C^\omega\)</span>, etc.), depending on the structure one wishes to impose.</p></li>
<li><p><strong>Whitney’s Theorem</strong> states that, for <span class="math inline">\(k \geq 1\)</span>, every <em>maximal</em> <span class="math inline">\(C^k\)</span>-atlas contains a <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-atlas, and that the resulting smooth structure is unique up to diffeomorphism. Hence, for <span class="math inline">\(k \geq 1\)</span>, nothing is lost by working directly with <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-manifolds. For <span class="math inline">\(k = 0\)</span> the analogous statement fails: there exist topological manifolds admitting no smooth structure at all.</p></li>
</ul></div></div><div class="dg-fn" id="fn-5"><a class="dg-fn-num" href="#fnref-5" aria-label="Back to the text">5</a><div class="dg-fn-body"><p>It is important to emphasize that it is possible to define two atlases, <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_2\)</span>, on the same topological space <span class="math inline">\(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\)</span> that are both internally <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible, but not compatible with each other. In other words, the union <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_1 \cup \mathcal{A}_2\)</span> does not form a valid <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-atlas because the chart transition maps between charts from <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_1\)</span> and <span class="math inline">\(\mathcal{A}_2\)</span> are not smooth. In that case, each atlas defines a different smooth structure on the same topological manifold. These are then regarded as two distinct smooth manifolds with the same underlying topological space but different smooth structures. This is not just a pathological possibility: there exist topological manifolds that admit multiple inequivalent smooth structures. A famous example is <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^4\)</span>, which admits uncountably many non-diffeomorphic smooth structures, known as <em>exotic <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^4\)</span>’s</em>. These are topologically homeomorphic to the standard <span class="math inline">\(\mathbb{R}^4\)</span> but not diffeomorphic to it or to each other. Another classical example is the 7-dimensional sphere <span class="math inline">\(S^7\)</span>, for which John Milnor discovered in 1956 the existence of <em>exotic spheres</em>, i.e., smooth structures on <span class="math inline">\(S^7\)</span> that are not diffeomorphic to the standard round sphere. Kervaire and Milnor later showed that <span class="math inline">\(S^7\)</span> admits exactly 28 smooth structures up to orientation-preserving diffeomorphism (15 if orientation-reversing diffeomorphisms are also allowed). For this reason, when defining a smooth manifold, one should consider not just an arbitrary <span class="math inline">\(C^\infty\)</span>-compatible atlas but rather the entire collection of charts that are smoothly compatible with it. This ensures that the smooth structure is fully specified. If two atlases are not compatible, they belong to different maximal atlases and define distinct smooth structures on the same topological space.</p></div></div></div>
```
